9
In which situation is total linear momentum always conserved?
A
in all collisions between two objects
B
in collisions between two objects moving at equal and opposite velocity
C
in collisions between two objects that form an isolated system
D
in collisions between two objects with the same mass

hints: Notice the word always and the phrase isolated system in option C compared with the mass and velocity details in the other options.
Recall that total momentum $p$ changes only if a resultant external force acts, with $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$.
Check which option guarantees zero resultant external force, so that the two collision forces are equal, opposite and internal only.
walkthrough: Identify the quantity: total linear momentum is the vector sum $p_{total} = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$ for the two objects.
State the governing rule: total momentum is conserved if the resultant external force on the system is zero, which is the definition of an isolated system.
Explain the collision: during contact the objects exert equal and opposite internal forces by Newton's third law, so their impulses $F\Delta t$ and $-F\Delta t$ cancel.
Test the other conditions: equal mass or equal and opposite velocity describe the objects, not the external forces, and many real collisions have friction or other external forces.
Therefore only the guarantee of an isolated system makes conservation certain. This is option C.

A.explanation: Not all two-object collisions are isolated - an external resultant force such as friction can change total momentum.

B.explanation: Equal and opposite velocity only makes the initial total zero in a special case, it does not guarantee no external force acts.

C.explanation: An isolated system has no resultant external force, so internal collision forces cancel and total $p = mv$ is unchanged.

D.explanation: Equal masses affect how velocities share out, but do not remove external forces, so momentum is not automatically conserved.
